n: Sound the alarm! Joel calls for the trumpet to warn the people in Jerusalem that the day of the Lord is coming. A trumpet blast was the ancient warning signal of approaching danger.

f.g: Hebrew shofar — a ram’s horn used for alarms and sacred gatherings.
Mount Zion, where the temple stood in Jerusalem.

n: That day will be dark and gloomy. A vast, powerful army will spread over the mountains like the dawn — unlike anything before or after. The locusts now foreshadow a greater, final judgment.

f.w: A day of darkness and of gloominess

n: This army devours everything like fire. Before it the land is lush like Eden; behind it, only wasteland. The image reverses the creation story.
They look like horses and charge like cavalry. A locust’s head really does resemble a small horse’s head.
Their noise is like rumbling chariots and crackling fire in dry stubble — an army lined up for battle.

f.g: Dry stalks left in a field after harvest; it burns fast.

n: People are terrified when they see this army coming; their faces turn pale with fear.

f.g: Probably “grow pale” or “lose their color” with fear.

n: The army is disciplined. Each soldier stays in line, climbing walls and marching without breaking ranks.
No one pushes another; they cannot be stopped even by weapons. Swarming locusts were nearly impossible to fight.
They pour through the city, over walls and houses, and in through windows like thieves. Nowhere is safe from them.
Earth and heaven shake; sun, moon, and stars go dark. These cosmic signs show that this is God’s great day.

f.w: the sun and the moon shall be dark

n: The surprise: the Lord Himself leads this army. It carries out His word. Joel asks, “Who can endure that day?”
Yet it is not too late! The Lord pleads, “Turn to me with all your heart.” Even in judgment, God’s deepest desire is for His people to come back to Him.

f.w: turn ye even to me with all your heart

n: Real repentance is inward. Tearing clothes was a sign of grief, but God wants a broken heart, not a show. He is gracious, merciful, and ready to hold back punishment.

f.w: rend your heart, and not your garments
gracious and merciful, slow to anger

n: Who knows? Perhaps the Lord will turn and leave a blessing — even enough harvest to offer at the temple again. Joel does not presume, but he hopes.
Joel repeats the call: sound the trumpet, but this time to gather for a holy fast rather than to sound alarm.
Everyone must come — elders, children, even nursing babies and newlyweds who were normally excused from duties. Repentance is for the whole community.
The priests stand between the temple porch and the altar and plead: spare your people, so the nations cannot mock and ask, “Where is their God?”

f.w: between the porch and the altar
f.g: The courtyard area just in front of the temple building, where priests ministered.

n: The turning point of the book: the Lord responds with zeal and compassion for His land and people.

f.g: Zealous, deeply protective of what is His.

n: God promises to restore food — grain, wine, and oil — so they will be satisfied and no longer be laughed at by other nations.
The “northern army” will be driven away into the desert, with its front in the Dead Sea and its back in the Mediterranean, and its rotting stench will rise. Locust swarms often died in the sea.
The land, which had “mourned,” is now told to rejoice, for the Lord, not the locusts, will do great things.
Even the animals can stop fearing; pastures are green again and trees bear fruit. Joel reverses each loss described in chapter 1.

f.w: the fig tree and the vine

n: Rain will come in its seasons. In Israel the “former” rains of autumn soften the soil for planting, and the “latter” rains of spring ripen the crops.

f.g: Some translate “the teacher of righteousness” — the Hebrew moreh can mean both “early rain” and “teacher.”

n: Threshing floors will be heaped with grain, and the vats will overflow with wine and oil — abundance replacing famine.

f.g: Vats — the troughs that catch juice from a winepress.
Threshing floors, where grain was separated from chaff.

n: One of the Bible’s most tender promises: God will restore the years the locusts devoured. He can redeem lost time and heal what was ruined.

f.w: I will restore to you the years
f.g: Many find personal hope here: the Lord can make up for losses — even those caused by sin — when we turn to Him.

n: The people will eat their fill and praise the God who acted with wonders. Their shame will be removed for good.
The greatest gift is not food but God’s presence: they will know He dwells among Israel and that there is no other God.

f.w: I am in the midst of Israel

n: A famous promise: God will pour out His Spirit on all kinds of people, and they will prophesy, dream, and see visions. Peter quoted this at Pentecost, and Moroni told Joseph Smith it was soon to be fulfilled.

f.w: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh
your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

n: Even servants — men and women of the lowest social rank — will receive the Spirit. God’s gifts are not limited by class or gender.
God will show signs in heaven and on earth: blood, fire, and columns of smoke, signaling that His great day is near.
The sun will go dark and the moon turn red as blood before the Lord’s great day. Latter-day Saints see this among the signs preceding the Second Coming.
Whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Deliverance will be found in Zion and Jerusalem. Paul applied this to calling on Jesus Christ.

f.w: whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered
in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance
